en.title: Redfall's Creators Explain What Went Wrong with the Failed Xbox Exclusive
en.summary: Former Arkane bosses Harvey Smith and Ben Horne are opening up about the troubled development of **Redfall**. They acknowledge the vampire shooter was a difficult project that struggled to find its footing.
en.body:
The dream of a compelling vampire-hunting RPG on Xbox soured dramatically with the launch of **Redfall**. Now, key figures from its development are shedding light on the missteps that led to the game's widely acknowledged failure. **Harvey Smith**, former director, and **Ben Horne**, former producer at Arkane Austin, have moved on to form a new studio, **Black Pony Immersive**, focusing on "imaginative first-person action-RPGs." Their recent comments reveal a project that wrestled with industry trends and unforeseen obstacles.

**Redfall** was conceived during a period of intense focus on live-service games, a genre that Arkane, known for its meticulously crafted single-player experiences like **Dishonored** and **Prey**, had not previously explored. "The team had to figure out, 'How do we do this?'" Horne explained. Smith admitted that Arkane "got swept up in the games-as-a-service thing," believing they could integrate its mechanics into their specialized formula. "I had the foolish chutzpah to assume that it always works out for us. We can do this. Let’s take what we love, and mix it with [games-as-a-service]," Smith reflected. The ambition included features like day-night cycles and character classes, aiming for a broader audience. However, development was further complicated by the **COVID-19 pandemic** and the subsequent "great resignation," which disrupted workflows and led to talent changes.

## Behind the Vampire's Bite

The critical reception for **Redfall** was harsh, with many pointing to a formulaic gameplay loop and significant technical issues. The game launched to a disappointing player count and struggled to maintain viewership on platforms like Twitch, a stark contrast to Arkane's previous successes. Xbox head **Phil Spencer** himself described the launch as a "knockback" for Microsoft and issued an apology. Despite the poor reception, the Arkane Austin team dedicated the following year to patching and improving the game. Even after Microsoft shuttered Arkane Austin and laid off the staff, Smith and a small group pitched Microsoft on releasing a planned 1.4 update, a testament to their commitment to the project they had poured so much into.

## The Fallout for Fans

For players who invested in **Redfall**, the outcome was undoubtedly disheartening. Many fans felt the game failed to live up to the pedigree of Arkane Studios, a developer renowned for its immersive sims and player agency. The promise of a unique, co-op vampire shooter was overshadowed by technical problems and a perceived lack of polish. The subsequent closure of Arkane Austin brought a definitive end to any hope of further significant updates, leaving the game in a state that many felt was never fully realized. This situation highlights the risks inherent in pursuing live-service models, especially for studios with a distinct identity.

## What's Next

Smith and Horne's new venture, **Black Pony Immersive**, signals a return to their core strengths in first-person action-RPGs. While no specific projects have been detailed, their focus suggests a renewed commitment to the kind of deep, engaging experiences their fans have come to expect, hopefully avoiding the pitfalls that plagued **Redfall**.

content_raw: Former Arkane bosses Harvey Smith and Ben Horne have opened a new studio, Black Pony Immersive, which is now working on "imaginative first-person action-RPGs." The last game they worked on was the ill-fated Xbox-exclusive vampire game, Redfall. Both Smith (Redfall director) and Horne (Redfall producer) have now discussed that project and what went wrong. Horne told The Game Business that Redfall was born during the live-service boom, and the team had to figure out, "How do we do this?" Smith added that Redfall was a "difficult project" for Arkane, acknowledging that the studio "got swept up in the games-as-a-service thing." "Arkane is very specialized, but the industry is growing, and there’s always more mouths to feed. And it’s great when you can reach a wider audience. I had the foolish chutzpah to assume that it always works out for us. We can do this. Let’s take what we love, and mix it with [games-as-a-service]. And do different mechanics by day and night. And have character classes," he said. During the middle of development, the COVID-19 pandemic broke out, which Smith said impacted Redfall. He also singled out "the great resignation" having an impact, as people started working remotely and changed jobs. Smith said Redfall was "very poorly received" at launch, with the team then spending the year next patching the game in an effort to improve it. Then Microsoft closed Arkane Austin and laid the team off. The team had even more improvements planned for a 1.4 update, so Smith pitched Microsoft on the idea of coming back to release this update, even though he just got laid off. "We went to Microsoft and said, ‘I know we don’t work here anymore, but can we please release this?’ And to their credit, they did not say no. They let six or seven of us sign forms that we could come back in the building. After being fired, we released 1.4, which I think if we had that on day one, it wouldn’t have set the world on fire, but it was a much, much better game," he said. Horne, for his part, said it was "like an achievement unlocked" in his professional career to release an update for a game "after I've been fired and the studio closed down." Also in the interview, Smith acknowledged that he was "clearly out of my lane" working on a live-service game like Redfall. "I was not working on the things that I should be working on." "Politically, there were very hard things. There were fires. The government announced aliens at some point. There was a swarm of murder hornets coming toward Texas. We had an ice storm that put power and water out for like two weeks for some people. It was crazy," he said. "That development cycle, I’ll never forget it. And yet at the end of it, people came back together to release that patch even after losing their jobs. And some of them wanted to work with us again after that."
